answer_text:
Assume \(p>1\) (so \(n\ge 1\)), and count positive integer solutions \((b,c)\) with \(\gcd(b,c)=1\).

Since \(p\) is odd and

\[
p^2+b^2=c^2,
\]

we have \(c^2-b^2=p^2\). Because \(p^2\) is odd, \(b\) and \(c\) have opposite parity. Modulo \(4\), \(b\) cannot be odd, so \(b\) is even and \(c\) is odd.

Now set

\[
x=c-b,\qquad y=c+b.
\]

Then \(x,y\) are positive odd integers with \(x<y\), and

\[
xy=(c-b)(c+b)=c^2-b^2=p^2.
\]

Also,

\[
\gcd(x,y)=1.
\]

Indeed, any common divisor of \(x\) and \(y\) divides their sum \(2c\) and difference \(2b\); since \(x,y\) are odd, it divides both \(b\) and \(c\), so it must be \(1\).

Conversely, any pair of positive odd coprime factors \(x<y\) of \(p^2\) gives

\[
b=\frac{y-x}{2},\qquad c=\frac{y+x}{2},
\]

and then \(p^2+b^2=c^2\) with \(\gcd(b,c)=1\). Thus solutions are in bijection with coprime factorizations

\[
p^2=xy,\qquad x<y.
\]

Write

\[
p=\prod_{i=1}^n q_i^{a_i},
\]

where the \(q_i\) are the distinct prime divisors of \(p\). Then

\[
p^2=\prod_{i=1}^n q_i^{2a_i}.
\]

For \(x\) and \(y\) to be coprime, each full prime power \(q_i^{2a_i}\) must go entirely to either \(x\) or \(y\). Thus each of the \(n\) prime powers has \(2\) choices, giving \(2^n\) ordered coprime factor pairs \((x,y)\).

Since \(p>1\), we never have \(x=y\), so exactly half of these ordered pairs satisfy \(x<y\). Therefore the number of primitive triples is

\[
\boxed{2^{\,n-1}}.
\]

(If one allows the degenerate case \(p=1\), so \(n=0\), then there are no positive primitive triples.)
